item.title: Undoing Brexit is the right thing to attempt – but sadly, I can't see Andy Burnham pulling it off | Paul Taylor
item.description:
Brussels rolled out a warm welcome for the PM but toxic UK politics around rejoining have not gone away

Despite the beaming smiles and the symbolic triple handshake, the summit intended to reset the UK’s tortured relationship with the EU showed just how difficult undoing Brexit will be a decade after Britons voted to leave.

To be sure, Brussels laid on a warm welcome. Andy Burnham’s first summit with the heads of the EU institutions felt like the homecoming of an old friend who had been away too long, rather than a meeting to settle some awkward leftovers of a bitter divorce.

Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Race to find survivors after Russian attack on apartment block kills at least nine
item.description:
A child pulled out alive after overnight strike in Dymer north of Kyiv; UN mission calls for investigation into attack that sank Russian warship in Libya. What we know on day 1,734

Rescuers in Ukraine raced on Monday to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike, after overnight attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 12 people. A strike on Dymer, about 45km north of the capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least nine people, according to Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko. Rescuers had recovered the body of another person from beneath the rubble and the death toll had risen to nine, he said on Telegram. The dead included a teenager and a woman in her 40s, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES) said earlier. Rescuers pulled out a child alive on Sunday evening, Tkachenko said. The SES said earlier it was searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”. “When [the explosion came], I literally flipped over in bed,” said Mykola Osadnyi, a relative of some of the missing who lived nearby. “My father-in-law … was screaming: ‘Save me, I’m burning!’” Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets called the attack part of “Russia’s genocidal war against Ukraine”.

In Vyshneve, two people were killed and eight wounded when a Russian strike hit a supermarket. “People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries,” Tkachenko said. One more person was killed when a strike set a private home ablaze in Bila Tserkva, he added. Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukrainian prime minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.

A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck early on Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. The strike – more than 1,000 miles from southern Ukraine – severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government, report Dan Sabbagh and Angelique Chrisafis. Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike. The UN mission in Libya (Unsmil) expressed “serious concern” over the drone attacks and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”, in a post on X.

Polish authorities say they have identified three flying objects that hit the country’s south-east as Russian cruise missiles, as Nato prepared to meet about an incident that Polish prime minister Donald Tusk called an “intentional provocation”. The prosecutor’s office in the city of Lublin said on Sunday that examination of fragments of the missiles that fell on Friday in the villages of Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik and Molodycz showed they were all Russian Kh-101 missiles. No one was injured when the missiles hit, though one impact was followed by an explosion and fire. Nato allies will meet in Brussels on Monday to discuss the incident. The missiles fell close to where thousands of troops from the European “coalition of the willing” – set up to support Ukraine – were holding exercises.

Denmark has expelled a Russian official after it said it had thwarted an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian American rapper at a concert on Danish soil. The case took a new twist on Sunday when Polish authorities revealed that the same man, Albert Vasiliev, was allegedly targeted by Moscow’s intelligence services last summer in Poland. Denmark is reportedly expected to ask the European Union this week for more decisive action stemming from the case.

item.title: US intelligence chief says he trusts Trump’s description of Putin as ‘my friend’
item.description:
Jay Clayton was pressed on Trump’s characterization of Putin during media appearances on Sunday

Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China.

Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. After a backlash at home and aboard, Trump doubled down on Saturday and posted a photo of himself and Putin shaking hands with the caption “My Friend.”

item.title: The Guardian view on Serbia’s new political era: a generational opportunity must not be wasted | Editorial
item.description:
Brussels must find ways to show concrete support for a new government that will genuinely share the EU’s democratic values

Following the extraordinary election that swept Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government from power, Serbia’s new political era has begun. Outside the National Assembly in Belgrade last week, large crowds celebrated as MPs from the victorious Student List movement were sworn in. Doctors, lawyers and academics put forward as candidates by the youthful protesters, who took on Mr Vučić, are now tasked with running an expectant country.

Their defining challenge will be to restore trust and democratic legitimacy in a nation that, under Mr Vučić’s bullying rule, plunged towards the bottom of Europe’s corruption rankings. Legal action has already begun against figures accused of illicitly profiting from the previous regime, while the new parliament’s elected speaker – a professor and organic farmer – called for the restoration of dignity and tolerance to its proceedings in his first address. Ensuring academic and media independence, and reforming the security services, which acted as the former president’s authoritarian enforcers on the streets, will be urgent priorities.
